profile.subject: Michelangelo
profile.overview: Michelangelo was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet who worked chiefly in Florence and Rome. He drew from living models and studied dissected bodies to understand how muscles change the outline of a figure in motion.

key_moments.title: A Pietà for a cardinal’s tomb
key_moments.text: In Rome, a French cardinal commissioned a sculpture for his tomb in the old St Peter’s Basilica. From **a single block of Carrara marble**, Michelangelo carved the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ in her arms.

key_moments.title: David by the town hall
key_moments.text: Michelangelo inherited a block of marble that another sculptor had already begun to shape. His **David** was meant to stand high on Florence Cathedral. When the statue was ready, the city chose a place for it outside the town hall, in the Piazza della Signoria.

key_moments.title: A new plan for the Sistine ceiling
key_moments.text: The contract with Pope Julius II called for twelve apostles and ornamental painting. Michelangelo asked for a different commission, and Julius let him plan the ceiling. Down its center, **nine scenes from Genesis** unfold inside a framework of painted architecture.

key_moments.title: An unfinished dome
key_moments.text: Pope Paul III had put Michelangelo in charge of building the new **St Peter’s Basilica**. He tested ideas for its dome with drawings and models. By the time he died, construction had reached the drum on which the dome would stand.

deep_facts.text: A sheet at the Casa Buonarroti in Florence preserves one of Michelangelo’s shopping lists. He illustrated the groceries as well as naming them. Among the items on the page are bread, herring and wine.

In Florence, Michelangelo designed a chapel to hold the Medici family’s tombs. He also worked for the republic that expelled the family. The hand that drew figures for the tombs drew plans for the city’s defenses.

connections.name: Pope Julius II
connections.connection: Julius commissioned his own tomb from Michelangelo, a project that produced the statue of Moses.

connections.name: Lorenzo de' Medici
connections.connection: Lorenzo took the young sculptor into his household in Florence.

connections.name: Sistine Chapel ceiling
connections.connection: Michelangelo returned to the chapel years after painting its ceiling to paint the Last Judgment above the altar.

connections.name: Leonardo da Vinci
connections.connection: Florence commissioned Leonardo and Michelangelo to paint battle scenes on opposite walls of its council chamber.

connections.name: Domenico Ghirlandaio
connections.connection: Michelangelo trained in Florence under the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio.

findings.claim: Michelangelo drew living figures and studied dissected bodies to understand muscles and the changing outline of a moving body.
findings.explanation: The exhibition connects his drawings from life and anatomical observation with his understanding of movement.

evidence.quote: Consistently dedicated to drawing the human figure from life, a growing practice in Florentine artists’ studios at the time, Michelangelo took this to a new level of verisimilitude through keen observation, as well as by studying dissected corpses to better understand the underlying muscles.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

evidence.quote: The dissections enabled Michelangelo to grasp how the surface and contour of the body change when one moves.

evidence.quote: Michelangelo completed the first half of the Ceiling, that is from the entrance wall to the Creation of Eve, in August 1510. The work must have been completed by 31 October 1512, as the Pope celebrated Mass in the Chapel on 1 November.

evidence.quote: The structure was designed by Michelangelo Buonarroti in 1546, during the pontificate of Paul III (1534-1549); the construction was halted when the artist died in 1564, at the height of the drum.

findings.claim: Michelangelo died before the dome he designed for St Peter’s was built.
findings.explanation: The Getty describes the state of construction at his death.

evidence.quote: Because of the project’s magnitude and complexity, Michelangelo did not live to see the finished dome; only the drum was near completion when he died in 1564.

findings.claim: An illustrated grocery list by Michelangelo survives at the Casa Buonarroti in Florence.
findings.explanation: Crack identifies the archived drawing, while McIver identifies its medium of communication and location.

evidence.quote: Michelangelo’s (1475-1564) illustrated list of groceries now preserved in the Casa Buonarroti in Florence (Fig. 3).
evidence.origin: Peter Crack, A Renaissance Menu

evidence.quote: Caption: Michelangelo Buonarroti, Shopping List, 1518, Casa Buonarroti, Florence.
evidence.origin: Katherine A. McIver, Cooking and Dining in Renaissance Italy

evidence.quote: Along with the list, Michelangelo included sketches of each item for clarification: the salad is in a wide, shallow dish
evidence.origin: Katherine A. McIver, Cooking and Dining in Renaissance Italy

findings.claim: Michelangelo’s illustrated list includes bread, herring and wine.
findings.explanation: Crack and McIver each describe these items in their analyses of the list.

evidence.quote: Michelangelo’s shopping list mentioned above also features a great deal of bread (Fig. 3). Anchovies likewise appear in both documents, although Michelangelo also enjoyed two servings of herring. Wine, soup, vegetables and two portions of tortelli complete the Florentine’s list of desiderata.
evidence.origin: Peter Crack, A Renaissance Menu

evidence.quote: For the first menu for two people, Michelangelo requested two bread rolls, a jug of wine, a herring and tortellini
evidence.origin: Katherine A. McIver, Cooking and Dining in Renaissance Italy

findings.claim: Michelangelo designed a funerary chapel for the Medici in Florence and drew figures for its tombs.
findings.explanation: The exhibition identifies the project and surviving figure studies, and the encyclopedia describes the sculptural commission.

evidence.quote: Two Medici popes—Leo X (Giovanni di Lorenzo de’ Medici) and Clement VII (Giulio de’ Medici)—provided Michelangelo with commissions centered on the family’s parish church, the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Florence. Michelangelo designed the architectural and sculptural elements for a New Sacristy, housing tombs of family members, and for the Laurentian Library (named for Lorenzo de’ Medici), adjacent to the church.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

evidence.quote: The tomb of Giuliano de’ Medici, Duke of Nemours was to be adorned with reclining statues representing Night and Day. Very few of Michelangelo’s drawings for sculpture survive, but four sheets related to Day offer rare insight into Michelangelo’s careful preparations on paper before taking his chisel to the marble block.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

evidence.quote: He worked (1520-34) on the sepulchral chapel of the Medici in the second sacristy of San Lorenzo, Florence, and designed the elegant, mannerist Laurentian Library which forms a part of the church.
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo

findings.claim: After the Medici were expelled from Florence, Michelangelo served the Florentine republic by drawing plans for the city’s defenses.
findings.explanation: The Casa describes the expulsion and his drawings. The museum biography and independent biographical entry corroborate his engineering work under the republic.

evidence.quote: In the first few months of 1529, alarming news spread through Florence, to the effect that the Medici Pope Clement VII was preparing, with the assistance of the Imperial army, to restore to power his family, expelled from the city on May 17 just two years earlier.
evidence.origin: Casa Buonarroti, Study of Fortification for the Porta al Prato of Ognissanti

evidence.quote: Assigned such an important post and encouraged by the esteem of his fellow-citizens, Michelangelo drew up a series of proposals for defending the gates in the walls.
evidence.origin: Casa Buonarroti, Study of Fortification for the Porta al Prato of Ognissanti

evidence.quote: Michelangelo Buonarroti Study of Fortification for the Porta al Prato of Ognissanti 1529-1530 circa pen and ink, watercolor, red pencil, 410 x 568 mm inv. 13 A
evidence.origin: Casa Buonarroti, Study of Fortification for the Porta al Prato of Ognissanti

evidence.quote: At the same time, he worked on the town's fortifications for the republican government, which had replaced the Medici seigniory.
evidence.origin: Museo Galileo, Michelangelo Buonarroti

evidence.quote: Michelangelo assisted (1529) as engineer in the defense of Florence
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo

evidence.quote: In 1527, Florentine citizens, encouraged by the sack of Rome, threw out the Medici and restored the republic. A siege of the city ensued, and Michelangelo went to the aid of his beloved Florence by working on the city's fortifications from 1528 to 1529.
evidence.origin: English Wikipedia, Michelangelo

counterevidence.quote: Alessandro and Ippolito left Tuscany; Caterina, on the other hand, stayed in town until the end of the siege. A Republican regime was thus restored

findings.claim: Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to design his tomb, for which Michelangelo made Moses.
findings.explanation: The museum identifies the patron, project and sculpture.

evidence.quote: The sculptural program for the tomb of Julius II, on which Michelangelo spent nearly forty years, produced the Moses, the Prisons in the Boboli Garden, the Slaves, now in the Louvre, and the Victory in the Palazzo Vecchio.
evidence.origin: Museo Galileo, Michelangelo Buonarroti

evidence.quote: In 1505 he was called to Rome to execute a sepulchral monument for Pope Julius II.
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo

findings.claim: Lorenzo de’ Medici brought the young Michelangelo into his Florentine household.
findings.explanation: The biographical entry describes his Florentine training and Lorenzo’s patronage.

evidence.quote: His early essays in sculpture attracted the attention of Lorenzo de' Medici, who took him to live in his household between 1490 and 1492.
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo

evidence.quote: He received the support of important patrons, including members of the ruling Medici family of Florence and, for a crucial decade, the leader of the Roman Catholic Church, Julius II.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

findings.claim: After his ceiling commission, Michelangelo received another to paint the Last Judgment above the Sistine Chapel altar.
findings.explanation: The Getty describes his later commission in the same chapel.

evidence.quote: In 1533 Michelangelo received a second commission for the Sistine Chapel, this time from Pope Clement VII: a huge fresco of the Last Judgment above the altar. The artist completed it in 1541.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

evidence.quote: The Sistine ceiling was executed between 1508 and 1512.
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo

findings.claim: Leonardo and Michelangelo received commissions for opposite walls of Florence’s Great Council Chamber, each depicting a Florentine battle.
findings.explanation: The Getty identifies the chamber, both commissions and the placement.

evidence.quote: In the summer of 1504, Michelangelo was commissioned to paint the Battle of Cascina on one wall of the Sala del Gran Consiglio (Great Council Chamber) in the Palazzo della Signoria, Florence. The commission brought Michelangelo into direct competition with Leonardo da Vinci, who had been contracted to paint the Battle of Anghiari on the opposite wall a year earlier. Both murals would commemorate famous battles in Florentine history.
evidence.origin: J. Paul Getty Museum, Michelangelo: Mind of the Master

findings.claim: Michelangelo was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio in Florence.
findings.explanation: The encyclopedia locates the apprenticeship and names the painters.

evidence.quote: After serving a year of apprenticeship to the painters Domenico Ghirlandaio and his brother David at Florence
evidence.origin: The Columbia Encyclopedia (1975), Michelangelo
